subject: chemistry

items.q: In the modern periodic table the elements are set out one after another in order of which quantity?
items.correct: Atomic (proton) number, going up by one at each step
items.misconception: Relative atomic mass, the larger number in each box
items.why: Relative atomic mass appears on every data sheet and usually does rise from left to right, and it genuinely was the ordering rule before protons were known. Check tellurium and iodine: mass falls but proton number rises, and the table follows proton number.
items.random_wrong: The number of occupied electron shells it has

items.q: Why is the table of the elements described as periodic?
items.correct: Because elements with similar properties recur at regular intervals
items.misconception: Because the table is revised at regular periods as new elements appear
items.why: Outside chemistry a periodical is something published at intervals in time, so the everyday meaning of the word is carried across. Periodic here describes the pattern in the properties, not the history of the table.
items.random_wrong: Because every row repeats the properties of the row above it

items.q: Chlorine and bromine are both in Group 7 and react in similar ways. What do atoms of these two elements share?
items.correct: The same number of outer electrons in an atom
items.misconception: The same total number of electrons in the whole atom
items.why: Students know a shared number causes the shared behaviour and reach for the only electron count they can name. Chlorine has 17 electrons and bromine 35; what they share is seven in the outer shell.
items.random_wrong: The same number of occupied shells in the atom

items.q: An atom of element X has the electronic structure 2,8,7. Where in the periodic table is X found?
items.correct: Group 7 and Period 3, from seven outer electrons
items.misconception: Group 3 and Period 7, reading its three occupied shells
items.why: Group and period are both position numbers and nothing in the words says which belongs to shells, so students attach the first number they meet to the first idea they meet. Read the structure twice: 2,8,7 has three occupied shells, so Period 3, and seven outer electrons, so Group 7.
items.random_wrong: Group 17 and Period 3, counting all the electrons

items.q: Rubidium lies below potassium in Group 1. From its position, what can be predicted about its reaction with water?
items.correct: It reacts more vigorously than potassium, giving off hydrogen gas
items.misconception: It reacts less vigorously than potassium, being a heavier metal
items.why: Heavier is taken to mean more sluggish, and the Group 7 trend is remembered in place of the Group 1 one. Lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball and potassium ignites: the reaction gets more violent going down.
items.random_wrong: It reacts to give rubidium oxide along with hydrogen gas

items.q: Before protons, neutrons and electrons were discovered, how did scientists attempt to classify the elements?
items.correct: By arranging them in order of their atomic weights
items.misconception: By arranging them in order of the atomic number
items.why: The modern rule is learned first, so it is read back into the history as though it had always been available. Protons were not discovered until after Mendeleev's table; he had only weights and properties to work with.
items.random_wrong: By arranging them in order of their outer electron counts

items.q: What problem arose in the early periodic tables when the strict order of atomic weights was followed?
items.correct: Some elements were placed in groups they did not belong in
items.misconception: Faulty weight values scattered elements far from their true partners
items.why: A rule that gives a wrong answer is assumed to have been applied to faulty data rather than to be the wrong rule. The weights were about right; the rule itself was the problem, as isotopes later showed.
items.random_wrong: The atomic weights themselves had all been measured wrongly

items.q: Mendeleev left gaps in his periodic table. Why did he do this?
items.correct: He expected undiscovered elements to fill them
items.misconception: He believed that no element could ever exist there
items.why: A gap looks like a permanent hole rather than a booking made for a guest who has not arrived. Elements with the properties he predicted were later found and filled those gaps.
items.random_wrong: He thought those places in nature were forever empty

items.q: Knowledge of isotopes helped chemists understand the periodic table. What exactly did it explain?
items.correct: Why an order based on atomic weights is not always correct
items.misconception: Why atomic weights could be measured far more precisely
items.why: Isotopes are associated with mass, so their role is assumed to be about better numbers rather than about a better rule. Argon is heavier than potassium because of its isotope mixture, yet it has fewer protons, so proton number is the sounder rule.
items.random_wrong: Why two atoms of one element hold different protons

items.q: Sodium reacts to form Na+ ions and sulfur does not form positive ions. What does this tell you about them?
items.correct: Sodium is a metal and sulfur is a non-metal element
items.misconception: Sodium is a non-metal and sulfur is a metal
items.why: Sign conventions are memorised without the electron-transfer picture, so the two signs get swapped. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a positive charge.
items.random_wrong: Sodium must be a non-metal, because it forms a positive ion

items.q: Which statement correctly describes where metals and non-metals sit in the periodic table?
items.correct: Most elements are metals, on the left and lower down
items.misconception: Most elements are metals, on the right near the top
items.why: Left and right are learned as a bare fact with nothing to anchor them, so the pair is easy to invert. Sodium, magnesium and iron are all on the left or centre; the right-hand edge holds oxygen, chlorine and the noble gases.
items.random_wrong: Most elements are non-metals, on the left and lower down

items.q: Which pair of properties would you expect a typical metal to show, in contrast to a typical non-metal?
items.correct: A good heat conductor that forms positive ions
items.misconception: A poor conductor of heat that forms negative ions
items.why: Sign conventions are memorised without the electron-transfer picture, so the two signs get swapped. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a positive charge.
items.random_wrong: A good conductor of heat, yet it forms negative ions

items.q: Magnesium has the electronic structure 2,8,2. How does this relate to its position in the periodic table?
items.correct: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, among the metals
items.misconception: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, on the right
items.why: Left and right are learned as a bare fact with nothing to anchor them, so the pair is easy to invert. Sodium, magnesium and iron are all on the left or centre; the right-hand edge holds oxygen, chlorine and the noble gases.
items.random_wrong: Two outer electrons put it in Group 2, identical to calcium

items.q: Why does magnesium react to form Mg2+ ions while chlorine reacts to form Cl- ions?
items.correct: Magnesium loses its two outer electrons; chlorine gains one
items.misconception: Magnesium gains six electrons and chlorine loses seven
items.why: The rule remembered is fill the outer shell, and gaining seven is the only way to do that from one. Losing one electron leaves a full shell underneath, which takes far less energy than gaining seven.
items.random_wrong: Magnesium has more protons than chlorine has in total

items.q: The noble gases in Group 0 are unreactive. Which statement explains this and describes their outer shells?
items.correct: Their arrangements are stable, eight outer but two in helium
items.misconception: Their outer shells are empty, so there is nothing left to react
items.why: Unreactive is heard as having nothing there, rather than as having nothing left to want. Argon is 2,8,8; the outer shell is as full as it can be, which is precisely why nothing happens.
items.random_wrong: Every one of them holds exactly eight electrons in the outer shell

items.q: Argon has the electronic structure 2,8,8. Why does argon not easily form molecules?
items.correct: Its outer shell is stable, so it need not share
items.misconception: It has already shared its electrons within a pair
items.why: Most familiar gases in the laboratory are diatomic, so the pattern is over-generalised. A stable outer shell gives no reason to bond, so noble gas atoms stay single.
items.random_wrong: Its atoms already exist joined together in pairs

items.q: What happens to the boiling points of the noble gases as relative atomic mass increases down Group 0?
items.correct: They increase steadily going further down the group
items.misconception: They decrease as the gases become lighter down it
items.why: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group and Group 7 reactivity decreases, so trend directions become a coin toss. Helium boils at about -269 C and radon well above -100 C: the values climb going down.
items.random_wrong: They stay the same, as these gases are stable

items.q: Boiling points in Group 0 are helium -269 C, neon -246 C, argon -186 C. Predict the boiling point of krypton.
items.correct: About -153 C, carrying the rise further down
items.misconception: Below -269 C, continuing past helium at the top
items.why: Group 1 reactivity increases down the group and Group 7 reactivity decreases, so trend directions become a coin toss. Helium boils at about -269 C and radon well above -100 C: the values climb going down.
items.random_wrong: About -230 C, falling below argon down the group

items.q: The Group 1 elements are known as the alkali metals. Which feature of their atoms gives them their characteristic properties?
items.correct: Their atoms each have a single electron in the outer shell
items.misconception: Their atoms each hold just a single occupied electron shell
items.why: Group and period are both position numbers and nothing in the words says which belongs to shells, so students attach the first number they meet to the first idea they meet. Read the structure twice: 2,8,7 has three occupied shells, so Period 3, and seven outer electrons, so Group 7.
items.random_wrong: Their atoms each need a single electron more to fill a shell

items.q: A small piece of potassium is dropped onto water. What are the products of the reaction?
items.correct: Potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas form
items.misconception: Potassium oxide and hydrogen gas are both formed
items.why: Oxide is the first metal-and-oxygen compound met, and the oxygen in water makes it look like the obvious product. The solution turns universal indicator purple because a soluble hydroxide, not an oxide, has been made.
items.random_wrong: Potassium chloride and hydrogen gas are given off

items.q: Lithium is burned in oxygen, and separately sodium is burned in chlorine. What are the two products?
items.correct: Lithium oxide, Li2O, and sodium chloride, NaCl, are made
items.misconception: Lithium oxide and covalent sodium chloride molecules
items.why: Halogens are non-metals themselves, so students expect them to share electrons with whatever they meet. Metal plus non-metal transfers electrons and gives ions; two non-metals share and give molecules.
items.random_wrong: Lithium hydroxide and sodium chloride solution

items.q: Lithium reacts steadily with water, sodium melts into a ball and potassium bursts into flame. Predict how caesium behaves.
items.correct: Even more vigorously than potassium, reacting explosively
items.misconception: Less vigorously than lithium, being the heaviest metal here
items.why: Heavier is taken to mean more sluggish, and the Group 7 trend is remembered in place of the Group 1 one. Lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball and potassium ignites: the reaction gets more violent going down.
items.random_wrong: About the same as potassium, as both are in Group 1

items.q: Why does the reactivity of the Group 1 metals increase going down the group?
items.correct: The outer electron is further out, so easily lost
items.misconception: Atoms lower down have many more electrons to give away
items.why: More electrons sounds like more to react with, and the fact that only one electron is lost is overlooked. Every Group 1 atom loses exactly one electron; what changes is how tightly that one is held.
items.random_wrong: Atoms lower down have more protons pulling on the shell

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the elements of Group 7, the halogens?
items.correct: Non-metals with seven outer electrons, found as pairs
items.misconception: Non-metals with seven outer electrons, existing as atoms
items.why: The symbol Cl is what appears in the data sheet, so the element is pictured as lone atoms. The halogens all consist of molecules made of pairs of atoms, written Cl2, Br2 and I2.
items.random_wrong: Metals with seven outer electrons, going about in pairs

items.q: Chlorine reacts with sodium, and separately with hydrogen. What kinds of compound are formed?
items.correct: An ionic compound with sodium, and a molecule with hydrogen
items.misconception: An ionic compound with sodium, and ions with hydrogen too
items.why: Having lots of outer electrons sounds like having lots to give away. An atom with a nearly full outer shell gains electrons rather than losing them, so any ion it forms is negative.
items.random_wrong: A covalent compound with sodium, and ions with hydrogen

items.q: Melting points in Group 7 are chlorine -101 C, bromine -7 C, iodine 114 C. Predict the melting point of astatine.
items.correct: About 300 C, continuing the rise on below iodine
items.misconception: About -150 C, since reactivity falls down the group
items.why: Reactivity falls down the group, so every trend is assumed to fall with it. Chlorine is a gas, bromine a liquid and iodine a solid at room temperature: the points climb going down.
items.random_wrong: About -90 C, dropping since reactivity falls

items.q: Why does the reactivity of the halogens decrease going down Group 7?
items.correct: The outer shell is further out, so gaining one is harder
items.misconception: Larger atoms are heavier, so they must react more sluggishly
items.why: Heavier is taken to mean more sluggish, and the Group 7 trend is remembered in place of the Group 1 one. Lithium fizzes, sodium melts into a ball and potassium ignites: the reaction gets more violent going down.
items.random_wrong: Extra shells lower down leave fewer outer electrons exposed

items.q: Chlorine solution is added to colourless potassium bromide solution. What is observed, and why?
items.correct: It turns orange, as bromine has been displaced
items.misconception: No change, as bromine is the more reactive halogen
items.why: Bigger is read as stronger, and the direction of the reactivity trend in Group 7 is forgotten. Add chlorine to potassium bromide and the solution turns orange as bromine is set free; the reverse does nothing.
items.random_wrong: It turns orange as bromine displaces the chlorine

items.q: An atom of element Z has 15 protons. Where in the periodic table is Z found?
items.correct: Group 5 and Period 3, from five outer electrons
items.misconception: Group 3 and Period 5, counting its three shells
items.why: Group and period are both position numbers and nothing in the words says which belongs to shells, so students attach the first number they meet to the first idea they meet. Read the structure twice: 2,8,7 has three occupied shells, so Period 3, and seven outer electrons, so Group 7.
items.random_wrong: Group 15 and Period 3, adding all its electrons

items.q: An atom of element Q has 19 protons. What does an atom of Q do when it reacts?
items.correct: Loses one electron to form a 1+ ion
items.misconception: Loses its outer electron, giving a 1- ion
items.why: Sign conventions are memorised without the electron-transfer picture, so the two signs get swapped. Losing negative electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion carries a positive charge.
items.random_wrong: Gains seven electrons to form a 7- ion

items.q: Does the number of neutrons fix an element's place in the table?
items.correct: The number of protons fixes the place; neutron number can vary within one element.
items.misconception: Elements are ordered by how many neutrons their atoms hold.
items.why: Protons and neutrons are taught together as the nuclear particles, so they get treated as interchangeable. Isotopes of one element share a place in the table despite holding different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is different between two isotopes of one element?
items.correct: They have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
items.misconception: Isotopes are atoms with different numbers of protons.
items.why: Isotope is remembered simply as different atoms of the same element, without which particle actually differs. Change the protons and you change the element, so only the neutron count can differ between isotopes.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Were Mendeleev's changes to the weight order mistakes?
items.correct: He swapped some pairs so that elements fell in with others of similar properties, and isotopes later explained why.
items.misconception: The swaps were errors that modern chemists have since put back into weight order.
items.why: Following the data is taught as good practice, so deliberately departing from it looks like cheating. The modern table keeps his swaps, because ordering by proton number puts those pairs exactly where he placed them.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are most of the elements metals or non-metals?
items.correct: The majority of the elements are metals.
items.misconception: Most elements are non-metals, since the everyday non-metals are the familiar ones.
items.why: Oxygen, carbon, nitrogen and chlorine dominate school chemistry, so non-metals feel more numerous. Count the table: the whole centre, left and bottom are metals, and non-metals occupy only a small block at the top right.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does every noble gas have eight outer electrons?
items.correct: All of them do except helium, which has only two.
items.misconception: Helium has eight outer electrons like the rest of Group 0.
items.why: The rule of eight is learned as universal, and helium's position at the top of the group hides its first-shell limit. Helium is simply 2: the first shell holds two electrons and is then complete.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What happens to reactivity going down Group 7?
items.correct: Reactivity decreases going down the group.
items.misconception: The halogens get more reactive further down, in the same way as Group 1.
items.why: One reactivity trend is learned and then applied to both groups without asking whether electrons are gained or lost. Chlorine displaces bromine from potassium bromide, and bromine displaces iodine, so reactivity falls going down.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which elements have similar properties, those in a row or those in a column?
items.correct: Those in the same column, that is, the same group.
items.misconception: Elements next to each other in a period behave alike because they are neighbours.
items.why: Nearness on the page is taken to mean chemical likeness, and rows are read before columns. Sodium and magnesium are neighbours yet behave very differently; sodium and potassium are a row apart and behave alike.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the formula of the compound sodium makes with chlorine?
items.correct: NaCl, because one sodium ion carries 1+ and one chloride ion carries 1-.
items.misconception: The formula is NaCl2, since chlorine is Cl2 as an element.
items.why: The diatomic formula of the element is carried over into the compound unchanged. The Cl-Cl bond breaks in the reaction, and charges of 1+ and 1- balance one to one.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.1.2 The periodic table
